title: "Is the banker's number right?" — pricing three in-licensed assets against a group that is already full
subtitle: A VP of corporate development arrives with a term sheet, a $740M risk-adjusted NPV and a board date three weeks out. Four phases later the package has two prices instead of one, and the gap between them carries a standard error. The dialogue is composed; every command in it was run, and every number in it was measured.
headline: You are not bidding on $744M. You are bidding on $241M — unless you buy the people too.
headline_note: The seller's valuation turns out to be reproducible: lift the FTE ceiling inside our own model, change nothing else, and the three assets are worth **+744 ± 144** $M of eNPV over ten years — a rounding error from the banker's $740M. Put the same three assets against our real **40 FTE** and they are worth **+241 ± 90**. The difference, **+503 ± 169 (2.97 se)**, is value the seller can legitimately sell and we cannot collect; producing that number is what the study is for. It is also actionable in exactly one way: 12 more development FTE are worth **−8 ± 91 — nothing measurable — bought on their own**, and **+370 ± 106** bought alongside the deal. So the term sheet is two cheques, the second one is the cheap one, and 24 FTE (**+306 ± 116**) cannot be told apart from 12. One number was withdrawn mid-session, and it came out of the analyst's own summary table rather than out of the engine: the row that read the interaction between the two cheques as a null. Re-derived from the arm-level ensembles it is **+378 ± 140, 2.71 se** — twelve people really are worth more once you own the assets — and the same audit sharpened the dose-response test rather than softening it. Every eNPV on this page is a horizon-truncated lower bound, which the model says itself, in a warning it raises on every arm.

hero.text:
**Bid against the realized number, not the standalone one, and put the 12 FTE in the same board paper as the deal.** The three assets return **+241 ± 90** $M against today's 40 FTE — conservative floor **$62M**. Fund 12 more FTE alongside them and the programme returns **+611 ± 101**, floor **$409M**, of which the capacity half alone is **+370 ± 106**, floor **$158M**. The same 12 FTE bought without the deal return **−8 ± 91**: a null. There is no reading of this study in which $744M is a price we can pay.

What produces the gap is legible in a single trace. The three assets land in month 8. At today's capacity they enter Phase II in months **25, 31 and 39** — the third sits on the shelf for 31 months. Fund the 12 FTE and two of the three start the month after close.

One number was withdrawn before the answer was delivered, and it came out of a hand-typed summary table rather than out of the engine: the interaction between the two cheques, which that table read as a null. Re-derived from the arm-level ensembles it clears at **+378 ± 140** — twelve people are worth that much more once you own the assets — and the turn that catches it is the one worth reading.

figures.caption: **The whole model, and the whole finding, in one picture.** Circles are pools — people, money, assets waiting at a stage — and boxes are the work that moves an asset from one pool to the next; an arrow into a box is a claim the work makes, an arrow out is what it produces. Gold marks a pool the run emptied at least once, which is to say a pool something had to wait for: **9 of the 11**, `fte` and every stage place. The two that stay hollow are the two that never bind — `cash`, because the budget is not the constraint here, and `own_p1`, the preclinical backlog, which never empties because it only grows. Every box in both pipelines, ours and the acquired one, reaches into the same `fte` circle. Delete that one circle and the two pipelines cannot interact — which is precisely what a standalone valuation assumes.

turns.text:
I've got a term sheet in front of me for three clinical-stage assets out of a private biotech — one about to enter Phase II, two behind it. Their banker has a risk-adjusted NPV of about $740 million on the package and they are anchoring hard on it. My board meets in three weeks and I have to walk in with a recommendation and a number.

Here is my problem. Our development group is 40 FTE and it is already full. Every one of them is on our own pipeline — four preclinical programmes, four in Phase II, three in Phase III — and nobody in the building has been able to tell me what happens to those if we drop three more assets on the same people. Finance keeps rebuilding the DCF and getting the banker's answer back, which is not surprising, because it is the banker's model.

So: is the $740 million right?

**Phase 1 of 4 — framing.** I want to change your question before I answer it, because the one you asked has an answer you cannot use.

$740M is probably a fair *standalone* valuation. Standalone means these three assets developed by an organisation that has enough people to develop them. That is the number the seller is entitled to quote, and it is the wrong number for you, because what you are buying is not three assets — it is three assets *plus a claim on 40 people who are already busy*. One of your Phase III starts holds 10 of those 40 for thirty months. A Phase II start holds 6 for twenty-four. The acquired Phase II asset wants 6 of the same people for fourteen. Nowhere in a discounted cash flow is there a line that says *and then it waits*.

So the two questions I intend to answer are:

- **What is this package worth to *us*, at 40 FTE?** Not to a generic developer — to the group that would actually have to do the work.
- **If we bid, must we also fund the integration capacity, and what is that second cheque worth?**

Two decisions, two prices. I will price them separately, because the second one is the only part of this you can still change after the term sheet is signed.

Here is how I get the seller's number and yours out of the **same** model, which matters for the conversation you are going to have in three weeks. I build one baseline — our pipeline, our 40 FTE, no deal — and every scenario is that baseline plus one change.

| Arm | What changes | What it answers |
|---|---|---|
| baseline | — | our pipeline as it stands |
| **+ deal** | three assets appear in acquired Phase II at month 6 | what the package is worth to us |
| **+ 12 FTE** | headcount only, no deal | what capacity is worth on its own |
| **+ deal + 12 FTE** | both | the programme |
| **ceiling removed** | the people pool set to 4,000 | **the seller's standalone valuation, reproduced** |

That last row is the one to watch. If the people pool is large enough that nothing ever waits for a person, what is left is a per-asset risk-adjusted valuation — same assets, same probabilities of success, same costs, same discounting. It ought to land near the banker's figure. If it does, then the distance between that row and the *+ deal* row is not a disagreement with the banker. It is the price of your capacity, measured.

**Defaults I am proposing. Correct any of them and I re-run rather than argue.** Ten years in monthly steps, so 120 ticks. Money in $M, eNPV discounted at **8%/yr** applied monthly. Development budget $6,000M — deliberately set so that cash never runs out, because you told me the constraint is people, and if I let both bind we will not be able to tell which one produced the answer. Spend is still charged against the result at face value; it is capacity that is free and money that is merely expensive. 120 simulated decades per arm off root seed **2026**, paired, so a deal arm and its baseline see the same run of luck.

Two things I need from you, then I build.

**1. The integration cheque.** If you did fund capacity alongside the deal, what is the plausible ask — 12 FTE? I will run 4 and 24 as well, so the answer arrives with a dose response instead of a single point.

**2. Who goes first.** Under contention today, does late-stage work beat early-stage work? My default: our Phase III outranks the acquired Phase II, which outranks our own Phase II, and preclinical goes last. That rule decides who waits, and who waits decides the answer, so it is the assumption I most want you to look at.

turns.text:
12 is the number. That is what the head of development says he would need — two clinical leads and the rest supporting. Run the 4 and the 24 too; I would like to know whether we are under-asking.

The priority rule is right, and it is written down nowhere, which tells you something about this organisation. Late stage wins. Nobody kills a Phase III to start a Phase II.

But let me be straight with you about the $740 million, because you are going to have to get past it and so am I. That number is not a guess. It is a risk-adjusted DCF off comparable transactions, with stage-by-stage probabilities and a discount rate their bankers will defend line by line. I have signed off on numbers built exactly that way. If your simulation comes back and says the package is worth a third of that, my board will ask me why I believe a model with a random number generator in it over a valuation method the whole industry uses — and *because it accounts for capacity* will not be enough. I need to know **which one is wrong, and where.**

Also: three weeks.

**Phase 2 of 4 — the model is built, and I have arranged it so that nothing has to get past your banker.** Your board's question — which one is wrong and where — has a clean answer, and it is not *mine is better*. It is: **neither, and the difference between them is one line of the document.**

The uncapped arm and the realized arm are the same model. Same three assets, same probabilities of success, same monthly spend, same 8% discounting, same run of luck. One number differs: the size of the development group. If the uncapped run lands on the banker's figure, his method is not wrong — it is a special case of this one, the case where nobody waits. And the gap between the two runs cannot be a modelling disagreement, because there is nothing left for it to be except the ceiling.

Here is what I built, in your language.

| Piece | What it is |
|---|---|
| **40 FTE** | one pool. Work *occupies* people for the length of a stage and gives them back at the end — it does not consume them. People come back; money does not. That single choice is what makes this a capacity study rather than a budget study. |
| **Your pipeline** | 4 preclinical, 4 Phase II, 3 Phase III, and a discovery engine adding roughly four new preclinical candidates a year. |
| **The three assets** | one entering Phase II plus two behind it, appearing in the acquired Phase II stage at month 6 — worth 1,400 per launch against 900 for a home-grown one. |
| **A stage** | holds its people for the whole cycle — 6 for 24 months in our Phase II, 10 for 30 in Phase III, 6 for 14 in the acquired Phase II — draws its budget every month it is in flight, and at the end either advances the asset or kills it at that stage's probability of success. |
| **Who waits** | your rule: our Phase III, then the acquired Phase II, then our own Phase II, then preclinical. |
| **Intent** | every stage tries to start everything it can afford to start, every month. |

That last row is the one I would defend hardest. The seven advancement steps are deterministic in their *intent* to start work, so a queue in this model is never a queue I dialled in — it is only ever people. Had I made the start rate random I could have manufactured any backlog you liked, and you would have had no way to tell.

The whole study is **eleven pools, eight steps, twenty-nine connections, written as JSON** — no structured tokens, no custom code, not a line of Julia authored for it. That matters for exactly one reason, and the reason is your three weeks: **each of the nine documents differs from the baseline by one appended block**, so `diff` shows the entire intervention. The deal arm is `acq_p2 += 3` at month 6. The capacity arm is `fte += 12`. The programme arm is those two lines together. The two uncapped arms differ from their partners by the initial size of the people pool and nothing else. There is nowhere for a second, undisclosed change to hide, and you can hand the diffs to your own analysts without handing them a model.

Nine documents, all validated clean. Next I run the health checks — before the comparison, not after. I would rather show you a check that fails than a summary that does not.

turns.text:
**Phase 3 of 4 — the health report, and it is not clean.** Two of the nine checks did not pass, and I want you to have both of them before you have any numbers, because one of them is a real limit on what I can tell you.

**The baseline fails `transitions_fire`: 7 pass, 1 warn, 1 fail.** Three steps never ran — advancing an acquired Phase II asset, an acquired Phase III asset, an acquired filing. That is correct. In the baseline we never bought anything, so there is nothing acquired to advance. The check cannot know that, and the fix is not to touch the model; it is to run the same check on an arm that does acquire, which comes back **8 pass, 1 warn, 0 fail with all eight steps firing**. I am telling you this because the sentence *the diagnostics are green* is what a study says when it has quietly run the gate on the arm that happens to pass.

**Both arms warn `horizon_sufficient`, and this one you will have to live with.** At month 120 there are still 7 programmes in flight in the baseline and 9 in the programme arm, with pools still trending in the final quarter. Work that starts before the window closes and launches after it contributes nothing. **So every number I give you is truncated at ten years and is a lower bound, not an estimate.**

Now the mechanism, from a single simulated decade, so you can see the thing rather than a summary of it. The three assets land in month 8 in both deal arms. Then:

| Arm | The three assets enter Phase II in | People free at the end of a month |
|---|---|---|
| no deal, 40 FTE | — | 1 or fewer on 96 of 122 months |
| **deal, 40 FTE** | months **25, 31, 39** | 1 or fewer on 81 of 122 |
| **deal, +12 FTE** | months **9, 9, 25** | 1 or fewer on 52 of 122 |

**The third asset sits on the shelf for 31 months.** It lands in month 8 and starts in month 39. Fund twelve more people and two of the three start the month *after* the deal closes. You are not buying different assets in those two rows — you are buying the same assets two and a half years earlier, and on a discounted cash flow a month of waiting is never recovered.

One honest complication in that table, because you will notice it and I would rather you heard it from me. **The baseline is the most saturated arm of the three.** With no acquired work competing for anything, the group is packed tightly into its own pipeline, and a 6-FTE Phase II start cannot fit into the gaps a 40-FTE ceiling leaves. So the obvious metric — percentage of time the group is full — moves the *wrong way* when you buy the assets, for a fragmentation reason that has nothing to do with your decision. That is why every argument in my report is made from how long work waits and how many launches happen, and never from a utilisation percentage. The most quotable measurement was the one I had to throw away.

The execution map at the head of this memo is the other half of that story: nine of the eleven pools were emptied at some point during the run. The two that never were are the budget — which is the constraint you do not have — and the preclinical backlog, which never empties because it only grows. It peaks near **26** in a pipeline that opened with **4**.

The comparison battery is running now: 120 simulated decades per arm, seven paired comparisons. I can see the direction already and I am not going to quote it, because one decade of this system disagrees with the next by hundreds of millions and you would be defending noise.

turns.text:
Hold on. Your own health check **fails** on the baseline. I am going to be asked whether the model works, by people who would love a reason to stop reading. What am I supposed to say — it fails but it is fine?

And the other one bothers me more. Work still running when your ten years are up: is that not the banker's argument handed straight back to him? He would say the same thing — you cut off the cash flows early, of course you got a smaller number.

Three weeks. Where is the number?

**On the failing check, say this:** the model was asked whether every step of the process ever happens, and in the arm where we never buy anything, the three steps that develop the assets we never bought never happen. The check has no way to know that arm is a counterfactual. The same check passes on every arm that acquires. If it had passed on the baseline too, *that* would be the thing to worry about — it would mean the baseline was quietly developing assets it had never been given.

**On the horizon, I am conceding your point rather than answering it.** Every number below is truncated at month 120 and is therefore a floor. The place you can see it biting is the dose response: 24 extra FTE measure **+306 ± 116** against **+370 ± 106** for twelve — not because the thirteenth through twenty-fourth person do nothing, but because the extra work they start launches after the window closes and the ledger cannot book it. That cuts *against* the deal and against the capacity, not for them. It cannot rescue $740M, and it means every threshold I hand you is a floor on a floor.

**Now the numbers. Your banker is not wrong. He is right about a company that is not ours.**

Remove the ceiling — set the people pool to 4,000 and change nothing else — and the three assets are worth **+744 ± 144** $M over the decade. He said roughly $740M. I will take that as the model reproducing a competent standalone valuation rather than as a coincidence.

Put the same three assets in front of our real 40 FTE and they are worth **+241 ± 90**.

| Comparison | Δ eNPV, $M | se | se from zero | |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **standalone** — ceiling removed, with the deal | **+744** | 144 | 5.17 | clears |
| **realized** — the deal at 40 FTE | **+241** | 90 | 2.69 | clears |
| capacity alone, +12 FTE, no deal | −8 | 91 | 0.09 | **null** |
| capacity alone, +4 FTE, no deal | +117 | 90 | 1.31 | **null** |
| **integration** — +12 FTE given the deal | **+370** | 106 | 3.48 | clears |
| integration — +24 FTE given the deal | +306 | 116 | 2.64 | clears |
| **programme** — deal plus 12 FTE | **+611** | 101 | 6.07 | clears |

**The headline is the subtraction: +503 ± 169, 2.97 standard errors from zero.** That is the stranded value — the part of the banker's number that exists, that he is entitled to sell, and that we cannot collect, because collecting it requires people we do not have.

And it is not an accounting artefact. It shows up in launches. Over the decade the acquired assets reach market **0.533 ± 0.061** times at 40 FTE and **0.917 ± 0.072** times with the ceiling removed — a difference of **0.383 ± 0.094**, better than four standard errors. Four tenths of a launch does not happen. Nobody writes that down anywhere.

**Here is the part I would put in front of the board, because it is the answer to *which one is wrong and where*.** Two rows of the same experiment, differing in one number:

| The deal's effect on our own pipeline | own launches | own Phase II completions |
|---|---|---|
| **at 40 FTE** | 2.842 → 2.542, Δ **−0.300 ± 0.144** | 4.108 → 3.392, Δ **−0.717 ± 0.171** |
| **ceiling removed** | 4.575 → 4.708, Δ +0.133 ± 0.243 — **null** | 8.383 → 8.558, Δ +0.175 ± 0.360 — **null** |
| at 40 FTE **plus 12** | 2.842 → 2.808, Δ −0.033 ± 0.147 — **null** | 4.108 → 4.825, Δ **+0.717 ± 0.179** |

Taking these three assets at today's capacity costs a third of one of our own launches and three quarters of one of our own Phase II completions, both measured clear of the noise. Remove the ceiling and both costs vanish into it. **Nothing changed between those two rows except the size of the people pool** — not the assets, not the probabilities, not the discount rate, not the random stream. That is not a model arguing with a DCF. That is the crowd-out your DCF has no place to put, isolated to one line of one file.

Fund twelve more people and the crowd-out is gone — and our own pipeline finishes *more* Phase II work than it does today, by the same margin it was losing.

One more reading, because it shows the model responding when it does not pay: 12 FTE bought with no deal pull the preclinical backlog's peak from **25.7** down to **16.1**. The people are doing something. It is just not worth anything measurable — **−8 ± 91** — because what they relieve is the front of a funnel whose launches fall outside the window. And I am not going to hand you a return multiple on capacity, in either direction: its stand-alone effect cannot be separated from zero, and anything divided by a null can be made to say whatever the author wants.

figures.caption: Six ways to spend the money, each with the margin of 120 simulated decades. The two hollow bars sit inside ±2 se — they are nulls, not small effects, and both of them are capacity bought without the deal. Read the widths as well as the lengths: a ranking only means something where the interval does not reach zero.

One simulated decade, month by month: people committed to work in flight, against the ceiling the board drew. The bid-only arm spends the decade pressed against 40 with the acquired assets queued behind it; the funded arm has 52 to spend and starts two of the three the month after close. Shading marks where the bid-only arm is within one person of its ceiling.

turns.text:
Now we are talking. Three things.

One — **this is the slide.** The people are worth nothing on their own and $370 million once we own the assets. That is a complementarity argument and it is a good one: the deal makes the hires worth something, the hires make the deal worth something, and that is exactly why the two have to be approved together instead of sequenced. My CFO will understand it in one breath, and sequencing is the thing he always tries to do to me.

Two — before I write that down, tell me where its error bar comes from. You have put a plus-or-minus on everything else, and I notice that one has not got one. It is a difference between two of your own differences. Do the two of them not share the same noise? I have watched people stack margins on margins until the answer was whatever they wanted, and if my CFO's analysts can pick that apart I would rather hear it from you first.

Three — I need **the number.** One figure I can put in a board paper with my name under it, and a walk-away. Not a range, not *it depends on the horizon*. If I go in with a plus-or-minus my CFO will pick whichever end suits him and quote it back at me for a year. So: **what do I bid?**

turns.phase: Before the answer — auditing my own table
turns.text:
**You asked the right question, and it caught an error of mine. Your slide is right — and I was one paragraph away from taking it off you on the strength of a mistyped row.** Here is the whole of it, because you should know how that number was formed before your name goes under it.

The claim has an exact form: what twelve people are worth *given* the deal, minus what the same twelve are worth *without* it. That is not one of the seven comparisons the tool runs. It is a **derived** contrast — a difference of two differences, assembled by hand out of measurements the tool made — and you are right that a derived contrast is exactly where a margin can be quietly stacked on a margin. In my working table that row read **+129 ± 169, 0.77 standard errors — a null**, and the paragraph I had drafted told you this study could not show complementarity at 120 decades.

So I went back and re-derived it from the arm-level ensembles instead of from my own table — `numbers.jl` in the study directory recomputes every published row straight from the envelopes, which is the job it exists to do. **The row was wrong in two places at once:** the value had been carried over from a different contrast, and the standard error was copied from the line directly above it.

Done from the arm means and their standard errors — each the mean of 120 simulated decades:

| Arm | eNPV mean, $M | se of the mean |
|---|---|---|
| do nothing | 985.0 | 58.6 |
| bid only | 1,225.9 | 67.7 |
| bid + 12 FTE | 1,595.9 | 81.9 |
| 12 FTE, no bid | 977.0 | 69.0 |
| ceiling removed, no bid | 1,269.9 | 84.4 |
| ceiling removed, with the bid | 2,013.8 | 116.3 |

> **Interaction = (bid + 12 FTE − bid only) − (12 FTE alone − do nothing) = +378 ± 140. 2.71 standard errors from zero. It clears.**

Twelve development FTE are worth **$378M ± 140 more** when you own these three assets than when you do not. That is your slide, and it is a finding rather than a framing. And to answer what you actually asked — where the margin comes from — a derived contrast's margin is the root-sum-square of the margins of the arms that go into it. Variances add. They add once per arm, and they never subtract, which is why the interaction's ±140 is wider than either effect it is built from and not narrower. I also checked the direction of the bookkeeping: a paired `effect` margin is exactly the root-sum-square of its own two arms' margins, to three decimals, on every comparison whose two arms I hold an ensemble for.

**Now the rule, which is the part worth keeping, because it is the rule my table broke.** You may difference two effects and combine their margins only when **the two effects share no arm.**

- **The interaction is safe.** Four measurements, four distinct arms, nothing shared, so the margins combine cleanly: ±140.
- **The dose comparison you asked for is not safe, and I had it wrong too.** Twelve FTE (+370 ± 106) and twenty-four (+306 ± 116) are both measured against the *same* bid-only arm. Combine those two margins as though they were independent and you count that one arm's noise twice: about **157**, too wide. Remove the shared arm and the honest margin is about **125** — a *sharper* test than the one I first ran, not a looser one. The difference between the doses is **64** against 125: **0.51 standard errors.** Twenty-four FTE still cannot be told from twelve, so the cheaper dose still wins, and now it wins on a test that could have caught a difference if there had been one.

**Where the error was, and where it was not.** Not in the model, not in the engine, not in any of the seven measurements — every envelope was correct. It was in a summary table I typed by hand from envelopes that were right. Nothing in `validate` or `diagnose` could have caught it: those check documents and runs, and a transcription error is neither. What caught it is the one property this study was built to have — **every number in it has a command behind it**, so a number can be re-derived from the thing that produced it rather than trusted because it is written down. If you take one process point out of these three weeks, take that one.

One limit on what I am now claiming, so nobody overruns it. **+378 ± 140** says the twelve are worth more with the assets than without, by more than chance, in this configuration and over this horizon. It does not license a multiple: I still will not divide anything by the capacity-alone effect, because that effect is a null (**−8 ± 91**) and a ratio over a null can be made to say whatever its author wants.

The bid number is next.

figures.caption: Every dot is one simulated decade. The two arms overlap almost completely — take one decade from each and you can get any answer you like, including the wrong sign — while the difference of their means, +611 ± 101, does not come near zero. This is the picture behind every margin on the page, and behind the audit in this turn: the width of one of these clouds divided by the square root of 120 is an arm's margin, and four of those margins combined are the ±140 that +378 has to clear.

turns.phase: The answer — what to bid, and what bounds it
turns.text:
**Open at $62M. Do not pass $241M on today's capacity. If the twelve FTE are approved in the same paper, the package supports up to $611M with a walk-away at $409M.** Four numbers, each a measurement, and here is which is which.

| The number | What it is | Where it comes from |
|---|---|---|
| **$62M** | the floor — what the assets return to us at 40 FTE on a deliberately pessimistic reading | realized **+241**, less twice its margin of **90** |
| **$241M** | the ceiling on today's capacity. Bid past it and you are paying more than the assets return to the group that has to develop them | realized, central |
| **$409M** | the walk-away with the capacity funded — the number I would defend line by line | programme **+611**, less twice its margin of **101** |
| **$611M** | the ceiling with the capacity funded | programme, central |

$744M is not on that table, and neither is $740M, because nothing we measured says we can collect it. That is not a claim that the seller is overreaching. It is a claim about us: at 40 FTE, roughly **$503M ± 169** of what they are selling lands in a queue.

**The two cheques, priced separately.**

**Cheque one — the assets.** Worth **+241 ± 90** to us as we are, floor $62M. Note what that floor means for your negotiation: the realized value clears zero by only 2.69 standard errors, so on today's capacity this is a deal that works but does not work comfortably. There is not much room above $241M for a premium, an earn-out and a bad Phase II.

**Cheque two — the twelve FTE.** Worth **+370 ± 106** *given the deal*, floor **$158M**, and **−8 ± 91** — nothing — without it. The gap between those two readings is itself measured: **+378 ± 140, 2.71 se**. That is the line that kills sequencing, and it is why both cheques belong in one paper: hired ahead of the deal, these twelve people cannot be shown to be worth anything at all. What they *cost* is yours to know and not mine — twelve development FTE over ten years is a number you have and the model does not. But if the present value of that headcount is under **$158M**, this is the best line item on the term sheet, and the only one on it that requires nobody's agreement but your own.

**Do not ask for twenty-four.** +306 ± 116 against +370 ± 106 for twelve: a difference of 64 against a margin of about 125 once the arm the two comparisons share is taken out of it — **0.51 standard errors.** Indistinguishable on a test sharp enough to have found a real difference, so fund the cheaper dose. The mechanism is the horizon, not the people: 24 FTE do start more work and the backlog peak falls further, but their extra launches land after month 120, where the ledger cannot book them.

**The one sentence for the paper**, if you want it in my words: *the three assets are worth $241M to us at today's capacity and $611M with twelve additional development FTE; both figures are lower bounds over ten years; the $744M standalone valuation is reproducible and not collectible by a group of 40.*

**What would change this, in the order I would worry about it.**

- **The priority rule.** Late stage beats early stage, and the acquired Phase II asset slots above our own Phase II. That rule decides who waits, and who waits produces every number above. It is also the one input you told me is written down nowhere. If development actually protects its own Phase II work in practice, the realized number moves and I would want to re-run before you bid.
- **The FTE loads per stage.** 6 people for a Phase II, 10 for a Phase III. If your real loads are materially lighter, the ceiling binds later and the stranded value shrinks.
- **The horizon.** Every figure here is truncated at month 120 and is a floor. If you want the ceiling rather than the floor, that is a longer run and a re-diagnose, and it is about a day. It would raise these numbers, not lower them — which is an argument for a longer horizon before you set the walk-away, not for paying more today.
- **What this is not.** Per-launch value and the stage probabilities of success are illustrative inputs, not diligence. What this study measures is the **gap** between a valuation that ignores capacity and one that does not, and that gap belongs to your 40-FTE ceiling — not to the price of these three assets, and not to any other company's pipeline.

One follow-up is a single document and one command each, if you want them inside your three weeks: the deal with the capacity funded at month 6 versus month 18, which prices *delay* rather than headcount, and the same package against a 50-FTE group, which tells you whether this is a story about these assets or about how thin we are running.

figures.caption: The reconciliation — four separate 120-decade measurements, not an inference. The seller's standalone +744 loses 503 to the 40-FTE ceiling, leaving the 241 the package is worth to us; 370 of that comes back if the twelve FTE are funded, landing on 611. Thick bar ±1 se, thin ±2 se. Note what the closure is and is not: the steps share their arm means, so the chain adds up as arithmetic for any four runs. It reconciles the two valuations; it corroborates neither.

turns.text:
**Editorial note.** The study this page walks through is finished, and its provenance is a file rather than a claim: `agent/studies/portfolio_bid/README.md` records the question, the nine documents, every command in the three batteries, and every number those commands produced. Nothing quoted in the conversation above is absent from it. What is composed is the **dialogue** — there was no VP of corporate development, and the exchange is written around the artifacts rather than transcribed from a live interview. The commands are the ones that ran. The numbers are 120-member measurements off root seed 2026, and they do not move when you re-run them.

Three things are on the page because they are the parts a polished demo cuts.

**The failing health check.** `rdx diagnose` returns 7 pass / 1 warn / **1 fail** on the baseline, and the failure is right: three transitions never spawn in an arm that never acquires anything. The check cannot know that, and the correct response is to explain it, not to suppress it — the same check comes back 8 / 1 / 0 on the arm that does acquire. The reason to leave it visible is that the alternative sentence, *diagnose is green*, is what a study says when it has run the gate on whichever arm happened to pass.

**The horizon warning, which makes every figure a floor.** Both arms warn that work is still in flight at month 120 — 7 firings in the baseline, 9 in the programme arm. That is not a footnote. It is visible in the results as **+24 FTE measuring less than +12**, and it is why the report hands over floors (Δ less twice its margin) instead of central estimates.

**The withdrawn row.** The only wrong number the session produced was in a summary table the analyst typed by hand: the interaction between the two cheques, entered as a null, with a value carried over from a different contrast and a standard error copied from the line above it. Every envelope behind it was correct. Re-derived from the arm means and their standard errors the contrast clears — **+378 ± 140, 2.71 se** — and the audit it triggered also corrected the dose-response test in the other direction, from a margin of 157 to one of 125, because the two dose comparisons share an arm whose variance was being counted twice. Both corrections came from the same rule, which is the transferable part: **two effects' margins may be combined only when the two effects share no arm.** Nothing in `validate` or `diagnose` could have caught a transcription error — those check documents and runs, and this was neither. What caught it was that every number in the study has a command behind it, so it could be re-derived rather than believed. That locates where this workflow is fragile: not in the simulation, and not in the ±2 se rule the CLI enforces on every metric, but in the tables and sentences assembled around the numbers afterwards. A model document can be validated. A hand-copied row cannot.

A quieter piece of the same discipline sits in the DIAGNOSE turn. The obvious way to display a capacity constraint is a saturation percentage — and on that metric this study reads backwards, because the **baseline** is its most saturated arm: a group with no acquired work is packed tightly into its own pipeline, and a 6-FTE Phase II start cannot fit into the gaps a 40-FTE ceiling leaves. The percentage moves the wrong way for a fragmentation reason that has nothing to do with the decision, so the argument is made from queue-wait and launch counts instead. The most quotable measurement in the study is the one that had to be dropped.

And the boundary, stated once. This is a study of a constraint, not of a price. Per-launch value and the stage probabilities of success are illustrative inputs, not diligence. What is measured is the gap between a valuation that ignores capacity and one that does not — and that gap belongs to the 40-FTE ceiling, the stage FTE loads and the priority order. Change those three and every number on this page moves.

appendix.title: Provenance — every number, and the command that made it
appendix.text:
`agent/studies/portfolio_bid/README.md` is the file that records this study: the question, the units and conventions, the eleven places and eight transitions with their FTE loads, cycle times and probabilities of success, the nine documents and the one `rules` block that distinguishes each, **every command in the three batteries**, and every number those commands produced — including the comparisons that came back null and the list of things the study does not support. Nothing in the directory was computed by simulation outside those commands, and nothing quoted on this page is absent from that file.

The study re-runs from a clean checkout. Three batteries in order — the seven paired `effect` comparisons, the seven `ensemble --per-seed` arm levels, then the two `diagnose` reports, three `run --trace` traces and the two `draw` diagrams — followed by `numbers.jl`, which re-derives every table in the provenance file from the envelopes (if the two disagree, the file is wrong), and `figures.jl`, which computes no simulation result: every value it draws is read out of an envelope written by one of those commands, so a figure cannot drift away from the number it illustrates. Run the batteries strictly sequentially; concurrent Julia processes contend on one package depot and block rather than compute.

footer: The study directory is `agent/studies/portfolio_bid/` — nine model documents, the `results/` envelopes every number here was read out of, and the `README.md` that records the exact command behind each one. The layer that ran it is `agent/`: `agent/README.md` for the CLI, `agent/skills/` for the four phases, `agent/reference/model_schema.md` for what a model document may contain — and this page is regenerated with `julia --project=. agent/scripts/render_session.jl agent/sessions/portfolio_bid.json`.
